newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW--CEL-SCI HIV strategy seen gaining.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW--CEL-SCI HIV strategy seen gaining.

text.p: The use of immune modulators as a second line of attack against HIV is likely to be adopted by more drug companies, the chief executive officer of CEL-SCI Corp told Reuters Thursday.

"This is the next thing in HIV treatment," said Geert Kersten. "The whole AIDS field is beginning to look much more at immunology and the next major improvements in treatment will be from additional immunology products."

CEL-SCI said June 3 it had begun a Phase I trial of its drug "Multikine," a mixture of hormones known as cytokines -- including interleukins, interferons and growth factors -- which work together to stave off infections.

In the study, to be conducted jointly with the AIDS Research Alliance in Los Angeles, 14 HIV-infected patients who are already taking protease inhibitor "cocktails" will receive Multikine injections over a three-month period.

The hope, Kersten said, is Multikine will jump-start immune systems of patients whose own immune hormones have been weakened by HIV, allowing them to fight off opportunistic infections and perhaps wipe out HIV viruses still lingering in the body despite cocktail treatments.

Thousands of AIDS patients have seen their health improve and HIV virus counts plummet during the past year with the introduction of protease inhibitors used in a cocktail combination with older anti-viral drugs like AZT.
"But that doesn't mean the virus has disappeared. It's still hiding out in parts of the body like the lymph nodes," said Kersten, whose company is based in Alexandria, Va.
"Immune system strength improves only minimally in patients that are taking these cocktails," he added.
Multikine is now in early clinical trials in patients with head and neck cancer and prostate cancer, Kersten said.

In another cytokine study, Chiron Corp is collaborating with the National Institutes of Health to design a large Phase III trial using a synthetic version of the modulator Interleukin-2 to treat HIV-infected patients.

Chiron last March said Phase II results of the NIH trial showed "substantial and sustained" increases in the number of CD4 cells, lymphocytes that stimulate production of a wide variety of cytokines necessary for a strong immune system.

Donaldson Lufkin & Jenrette drug analyst Alex To said he believed use of immune modulating drugs was "the next complement for AIDS treatment because protease inhibitors don't increase CD4 cells or immunity."
"But it is wise not to get too excited about any specific product near-term," he cautioned, because immune modulating drugs in general have a high failure rate in clinical trials.
